title: Cap. III Rat. 8: if not from foresight, majority would be elect — few are saved
latin: Rat. 8. Si Deus absque operum nostrorum praescientia praedestinaret, majorem saltem partem hominum praedestinasset ad vitam, cum sit natura bonus, et misericordia ejus sit super omnia opera ejus: At pauci sunt qui salvantur: Ergo non praedestinat Deus nisi secundum praevisionem operum sive boni aut mali usus liberi arbitrii.
pass_a: Reason 8. If God should predestine without foresight of our works, he would have predestined at least the greater part of human beings to life, since he is good by nature, and his mercy is over all his works: But few are they who are saved: Therefore God does not predestine except according to foresight of works, that is of the good or bad use of free choice.
pass_b: Rat. 8. Without foresight of our works, they argue, a God good by nature — whose mercy is over all his works — would have marked at least most of humankind for life. Yet few are saved. So predestination must track foresight of works, that is of free choice used well or badly.

lemmas.gloss: without foresight would elect the majority
few saved implies foresight of free choice's use

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 8: goodness wills some good to each — not equal goods by foresight
latin: Sol. Ex eo quod Deus sit natura bonus, recte infertur, illum velle bonum omni suae creaturae; sed non recte, illum velle quodvis bonum cuivis creaturae, aut aequalia et eadem bona aequalibus creaturis. Nec in Naturae quidem aut Fortunae falso dictis bonis dispensandis tenetur Deus aut haec dispensare ex praeviso bono usu eorum, aut ea majori parti hominum impertire. Videmus siquidem neque robur corporis, neque acumen mentis, neque formae venustatem, neque divitiarum affluentiam dari ex boni usus praescientia. Nam, ut plurimum, dantur illis, qui hisce omnibus pessime abutuntur, ad injuriam, ad fraudem, ad libidinem, ad luxuriam. Haec tamen ipsa bona non nisi paucis conceduntur.
pass_a: Solution. From this, that God is good by nature, it is rightly inferred that he wills good to every creature of his; but not rightly, that he wills any and every good to any and every creature, or equal and the same goods to equal creatures. Nor even in dispensing the goods falsely called of Nature or of Fortune is God bound either to dispense these from a foreseen good use of them, or to impart them to the greater part of human beings. For we see that neither strength of body, nor sharpness of mind, nor beauty of form, nor abundance of riches is given from foresight of good use. For, for the most part, they are given to those who abuse all these things most badly, unto injury, unto fraud, unto lust, unto luxury. Yet these very goods themselves are granted only to few.
pass_b: Sol. From God's being good by nature it rightly follows that he wills some good to every creature of his — not that he wills every good to every creature, or the same equal goods to equal creatures. Even in dispensing so-called goods of Nature or Fortune he is not bound to give them from foresight of good use, nor to impart them to the majority. We see strength of body, sharpness of mind, beauty of form, and abundance of riches are not given from foresight of good use — for the most part they go to those who abuse them worst: to injury, fraud, lust, luxury. And even those goods are granted only to few.

lemmas.gloss: wills some good to every creature

lemmas.lemma: bona Naturae / non ex praescientia usus
lemmas.gloss: natural goods not from foresight of use

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 8: electing the corrupt mass — no duty to choose the majority
latin: Porro, illud quoque observandum nos loqui de electione eorum ad vitam, qui sunt omnes morte aeterna dignissimi. Quamvis igitur admittamus Deum ex bonitate suae naturae velle omnibus hominibus, quatenus considerantur ante lapsum justitia et sanctitate ornati, donum illud aeternae vitae; nulla tamen ratio cogit ut dicamus, ex hominibus corruptis et in massa damnabili obrutis, Deum pro bonitate sua debere vel omnes, vel majorem partem eligere ad gloriam.
pass_a: Further, this also is to be observed, that we speak of the election to life of those who are all most worthy of eternal death. Although therefore we admit that God from the goodness of his nature wills to all human beings, inasmuch as they are considered before the fall adorned with justice and holiness, that gift of eternal life; yet no reason compels us to say that, from human beings corrupted and sunk in the damnable mass, God for his goodness owes it to elect either all, or the greater part, to glory.
pass_b: Further: we are speaking of election to life of people who are all most worthy of eternal death. We may grant that from the goodness of his nature God wills the gift of eternal life to all humans as considered before the fall, adorned with justice and holiness — yet no reason forces us to say that, from humans corrupted and sunk in the damnable mass, his goodness obliges him to elect either all or the greater part to glory.

lemmas.gloss: all most worthy of eternal death
goodness does not oblige electing the majority

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 8: mercy over all works — special mercy; few freed more illustrious
latin: Ad extremum, quod urgetur, misericordiam ejus esse super omnia opera ejus, ad rem non facit. Nam primo, potest Deus misericordiam exhibere omni homini (quod revera facit) et tamen non hanc specialem et eximiam misericordiam, ut illum adoptet in haeredem vitae aeternae. Secundo, magnitudo misericordiae Divinae non pensanda est ex multitudine individuorum quibus impertitur, sed ex magnitudine beneficiorum quae hominibus impertiuntur, et indignitate illorum quibus impertiuntur. Nam quod Deus ex inimicis suis, peccati labe contaminatissimis, et aeterna morte dignissimis, per mortem dilectissimi sui filii, quantumvis paucos voluerit liberare, et regno caelesti destinare, illustrius est specimen misericordiae, quam justitiae illud, quod totum mundum improbum relinquat merito exitio.
pass_a: Finally, what is urged, that his mercy is over all his works, does not make to the point. For first, God can exhibit mercy to every human being (which in truth he does) and yet not this special and outstanding mercy, that he adopt him as heir of eternal life. Second, the greatness of the divine mercy is not to be weighed from the multitude of individuals to whom it is imparted, but from the greatness of the benefits which are imparted to human beings, and from the unworthiness of those to whom they are imparted. For that God from his enemies, most contaminated with the stain of sin, and most worthy of eternal death, through the death of his most beloved Son, has willed to free however few, and to destine them to the heavenly kingdom, is a more illustrious specimen of mercy than that of justice, that he leave the whole wicked world to deserved destruction.
pass_b: Finally, the press that his mercy is over all his works misses the point. First, God can show mercy to every person (and he does) without that special, outstanding mercy of adopting them as heir of eternal life. Second, the greatness of divine mercy is not weighed by how many individuals receive it, but by the greatness of the benefits given and the unworthiness of those who receive them. That God from his enemies — most stained with sin and most worthy of eternal death — through the death of his most beloved Son has willed to free even a few and destine them to the heavenly kingdom is a more illustrious specimen of mercy than the justice of leaving the whole wicked world to deserved ruin.

lemmas.gloss: mercy-over-all does not force majority election
special mercy of adopting to eternal life
freeing few is brighter mercy than mass justice

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 8 close: Augustine — multitude of reject shows justice; Epist. 190
latin: Postremo, cur Deus qui posset omnes, paucos tamen prae multitudine rejectorum voluerit ad vitam praedestinare, duae rationes ab Augustino afferuntur, ut minime opus sit ad praescientiam bonorum et malorum operum confugere. Sic igitur ille, Hoc voluit Deus, ut ipsa rejectorum multitudine ostenderetur, quam nullius momenti sit apud Deum justum quantalibet numerositas justissime damnatorum: Atque ut suaderet ut hinc intelligant qui ex ipsa damnatione redimuntur, hoc fuisse debitum massae illi universae, quod tam magnae parti ejus redditum cernerent, Epist. 190.
pass_a: Finally, why God who could [save] all, yet has willed to predestine few to life before the multitude of the rejected, two reasons are brought by Augustine, so that there is least need to take refuge in foresight of good and bad works. Thus therefore he: God willed this, that by the very multitude of the rejected it might be shown how of no moment is, with the just God, any number however great of those most justly damned: And that he might persuade that from this those who are redeemed from that very damnation may understand that this was due to that universal mass, which they would see rendered to so great a part of it, Epistle 190.
pass_b: Finally: why God, who could save all, yet willed to predestine few to life against the multitude of the rejected — Augustine gives two reasons, so there is little need to take refuge in foresight of good and bad works. Thus he: God willed this, that by the very multitude of the rejected it might be shown how little moment any number of those most justly damned has with the just God — and that those redeemed from that damnation might understand from this that what they see rendered to so great a part of it was due to that universal mass (Epist. 190).

lemmas.gloss: number of justly damned of no moment with God
Augustine: due to the universal mass
